questions.stem: Efficiency is defined as the ratio of:

options.text: useful energy output to total energy output
options.explanation: This is the stated definition of efficiency.

options.text: total energy input to useful energy output
options.explanation: This is the reciprocal of the efficiency ratio.

options.text: useful energy output to total energy input only
options.explanation: The definition uses total output, which equals total input — but the stated ratio is to output.

options.text: wasted energy output to total energy output
options.explanation: That scores the WASTE, not the efficiency.

questions.stem: A motor receives 300 J and wastes 85 J. Its useful energy output is:

options.explanation: Adding the waste back inflates the total beyond the input.
Useful output = 300 - 85 = 215 J.
That is the wasted share.
That is the total output, not the useful share.

questions.stem: The same motor’s efficiency is:

options.explanation: This halves the useful share incorrectly.
No real motor converts every joule usefully.
That is the wasted share’s percentage, not the efficiency.

questions.stem: Why can the useful output of a device never exceed its total output?

options.explanation: Nothing doubles here.
The limit is a law, not an instrument artefact.
Overheating is a symptom, not the law.

options.text: because useful output can never exceed total output, which equals the input by conservation
options.explanation: The useful share is part of a conserved total.

questions.stem: A heater transfers all of its output energy into room heating. What does that make its efficiency?

options.text: all of its output energy is useful, i.e. ends up heating the room
options.explanation: For a heater, the intended output is heat, so an all-heat output is fully useful.

options.text: it wastes no energy as sound only
options.explanation: The claim is about ALL output, not one pathway.
Input is still required; only the split changes.
Nothing produces energy from nothing.

questions.stem: State the equation for efficiency as a percentage.
questions.modelAnswer: Efficiency is the useful output divided by the total output, multiplied by 100.

questions.stem: State the relationship between total energy input and total energy output, and the law behind it.
questions.modelAnswer: What leaves the device equals what arrives at it, because of the principle of conservation of energy.

questions.stem: Explain why efficiency can also be written as a ratio between 0 and 1, and state what a ratio of 0.4 means.
questions.modelAnswer: The × 100% only rescales the fraction; dividing useful output by total output is a ratio by construction, so 0.4 means 40% of the output energy is useful and 60% is wasted.

questions.stem: A different motor receives 500 J each second and wastes 150 J. Calculate its useful output and its efficiency.
What does the width of each arrow in a Sankey diagram represent?

options.text: the direction of the energy transfer
options.explanation: Direction is shown by the arrow shape, not width.

options.text: the amount of energy being transferred
options.explanation: Widths are proportional to the energy transferred.

options.text: the speed of the energy transfer
options.explanation: Sankeys show amounts, not rates of flow speed.
Temperature appears nowhere in a Sankey.

questions.stem: Which part of a Sankey diagram represents the useful energy output?

options.explanation: Labels describe; arrows carry the energy.
That is the energy input.

options.text: the straight arrow pointing to the right
options.explanation: The straight arrow is the desired, useful output.
Those are the wasted energy.

questions.stem: What does the flat left-hand end of a Sankey diagram represent?

options.explanation: The useful output is the straight arrow on the right.
Efficiency is a ratio of widths, not one arrow.
Waste bends away at the split, not at the flat end.

options.text: the energy transferred into the system
options.explanation: The flat end is the input side of the diagram.

questions.stem: On a Sankey diagram, which conservation equation do the arrow widths always satisfy?

options.text: what arrives = useful share + wasted share
options.explanation: The input splits exactly into useful and waste.

options.text: what arrives = useful share - wasted share
options.explanation: Waste adds, not subtracts.
The split need not be equal.

options.text: total energy in = 2 × useful energy out
options.explanation: No such doubling rule exists.

questions.stem: A Sankey’s input arrow is 10 mm wide, the useful arrow is 7 mm and the waste arrow is 3 mm. Which reading is correct?

options.explanation: The widths recombine exactly: 7 + 3 = 10.
Widths are proportional to energy, so 7 / 10 = 70% useful.
That is the waste share, not the efficiency.
Adding widths is meaningless here.

questions.stem: State what the arrows that bend away from a Sankey diagram represent.
State the two equations a Sankey diagram satisfies at its splitting point.
questions.modelAnswer: Input equals output, and the input splits into the useful share plus the wasted share.

questions.stem: Explain how a Sankey diagram shows efficiency without any numbers being written on it.
questions.modelAnswer: Because arrow widths are proportional to energy, the useful arrow’s share of the total width IS the efficiency: a wide straight arrow against a thin waste arrow shows a high efficiency, and the comparison works visually because conservation guarantees the widths always recombine to the input width.

questions.stem: A Sankey’s input arrow is 8 mm wide and its waste arrow is 2 mm. State the useful energy share as a percentage and describe what the useful arrow’s width must be.
questions.modelAnswer: The useful share is 75%, and the useful arrow must be 6 mm wide, because widths are proportional and 8 - 2 = 6 mm must close the balance.

questions.stem: A modern efficient bulb and an old filament bulb draw the same input. On their Sankey diagrams, the efficient bulb has:

options.explanation: Real bulbs still waste some energy.
Efficient means LESS waste.

options.text: a narrower waste arrow and a wider useful arrow
options.explanation: Higher efficiency shifts width from the waste arrow to the useful arrow.
Both draw the same input.

questions.stem: A Sankey shows 500 J entering and 120 J leaving usefully. The wasted energy is:

options.explanation: That is the useful output.
That is the total input.
Adding violates conservation; waste is what the input leaves behind.

questions.stem: The same lifting motor’s efficiency is:

options.explanation: This halves the useful share incorrectly.
A motor losing 380 J of 500 J is far from perfect.
That is the waste percentage (380/500), not the efficiency.

questions.stem: For an old filament bulb, most of the input arrow’s width:

options.explanation: Filament bulbs waste most energy as heat.

options.text: bends away as heat because the bulb wastes most of its energy
options.explanation: The filament bulb’s waste arrow dominates its Sankey.
Glass is not an energy store in this model.
Energy does not flow back up the supply.

questions.stem: Which calculation chain converts a Sankey into the device’s efficiency?

options.explanation: That is the reciprocal, which exceeds 100%.

options.text: wasted = input + useful, then efficiency = wasted / input
options.explanation: Both steps are wrong: waste subtracts, and efficiency divides useful by total.

options.text: wasted = input − useful, then efficiency = useful / input × 100
options.explanation: Subtract for the waste share, then divide useful by the total input.
That ratios the two wrong quantities.

questions.stem: State which arrow grows wider when a bulb becomes more efficient at the same input.
questions.modelAnswer: The straight useful-output arrow grows wider and the downward wasted-heat arrow shrinks.

questions.stem: In the lifting-motor Sankey, state the useful output and the total input.
questions.modelAnswer: The useful output is 120 J and the total input is 500 J.

questions.stem: Explain why the filament bulb’s Sankey and the efficient bulb’s Sankey can both satisfy conservation while looking so different.
questions.modelAnswer: Conservation only fixes the TOTAL width: input = useful + waste. The two bulbs split the same total differently — the efficient bulb gives the straight arrow most of the width, the filament bulb gives the waste arrow most — so both diagrams close their balance while telling opposite efficiency stories.

questions.stem: A second motor’s Sankey shows 800 J in and its waste arrow represents 560 J. Calculate the useful output and the efficiency.
